posts.raw_content:
No, members of Congress do not automatically receive or hold traditional security clearances. 

Reddit
·r/SecurityClearance
 +1
Instead, lawmakers bypass the standard executive-branch background check process. By tradition and constitutional design, they are deemed inherently trustworthy to access classified information simply by virtue of being elected to their office. 

Congress.gov
 +3
Key facts about how security and access work for Congress include:
No Background Checks: Members do not undergo the FBI or executive branch background investigations required for federal employees, military personnel, or contractors. 

Reddit
·r/SecurityClearance
 +1
Access vs. Clearance: They do not hold a "clearance" per se; rather, they have constitutional and traditional eligibility to access classified materials based on their role and a "need-to-know" (often tied to specific committee assignments like the intelligence or armed services committees). 

Roll Call
 +1
Oaths of Secrecy: Lawmakers take secrecy oaths upon taking office, and they can face internal congressional discipline—including potential expulsion by a two-thirds vote—if they leak classified information. 

WUSA9
 +3
Staff Are Different: Unlike the members themselves, congressional aides and personal or committee staff do have to go through formal background investigations and obtain security clearances to handle classified files. 

GovExec.com
 +2
For further details on how these rules are structured, read the Congressional Research Service FAQ on Security Clearances or examine industry perspectives on Roll Call.
